name: Admiral FFT
workload: Complex and real 1-D and N-D FFTs, float and double: 19 1-D lengths and 9 N-D shapes against FFTW_MEASURE (1 thread, both precisions pooled); 61 1-D lengths and 27 N-D shapes against ducc0.
claimed_speedup: 1.34x (1-D) and 1.43x (N-D) over FFTW_MEASURE at 1 thread; 2.18x (f64) and 2.70x (f32) over ducc0 for 1-D at 1 thread; ducc0 2-D 1.12x/1.41x and 3-D 1.60x/1.67x at 1 thread (ratios are reference time over Admiral time).
compiler_and_flags: GCC 14.2, -march=native, CMake release preset (benchmark/README.md, sweep of 2026-08-24); nanobench harness, min across repetitions, arm order alternated in A/B modes
hardware: Intel Xeon w5-3435X, 16 physical cores, AVX-512
tradeoffs: C++20 (buildable at C++17) with a compiled engine and three interfaces (C++, C, drop-in FFTW3 subset). Depends on xsimd and poet fetched by CPM. Codelets up to radix 64 make compile times long. No wisdom files. Threads stay serial below about 32k elements. Long-double runs scalar.
caveats: Very new project; the README says the code was largely produced by asking Claude to instantiate codelets with poet/xsimd and tune a cost model, and the author says he does not claim the fastest FFT. FFTW version is not stated (system fftw3 via pkg-config). No MKL comparison in the README. Threaded 1-D versus threaded ducc0 is mixed (0.33x to 1.82x by size, benchmark/README.md). Single machine. License is the SPDX BSD-3-Clause-Attribution (attribution clause); OSI status not confirmed. DiamonDinoia/fft_bench charts MKL/FFTW/KISS/Pocket/DUCC/Sleef/Admiral on three cluster CPUs but only as images, and its README says MKL threaded numbers before 2026-09-16 were invalid.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'github Highway OR xsimd FFT library FFTW comparison speedup radix codelets generator' surfaced DiamonDinoia/admiral; confirmed through the DiamonDinoia/fft_bench README, which lists 'Admiral' among benchmarked libraries

name: pocketfft-tuned (benchmark-driven PocketFFT fork)
baseline: FFTW3 FFTW_ESTIMATE, upstream PocketFFT (ref 32424d2) and KissFFT; the fork is slower than FFTW_MEASURE and KFR
workload: Randomized interleaved Google Benchmark sweep, 90 iterations per scenario, taskset -c 2: 14 mixed 1-D sizes (4096 to 1048576 including primes and near-primes), five 2-D shapes (256x256 to 1024x1024) and four 3-D shapes (64^3 to 128x128x64); c2c, r2c and c2r. Ratio is other implementation CPU ns over tuned fork CPU ns.
claimed_speedup: SIMD build, median ratio (tuned wins/ratios): 1-D c2c 2.40x vs upstream PocketFFT (1258/1260), 1.35x vs FFTW_ESTIMATE (813/1260), 4.63x vs KissFFT (952/990), 3.25x vs meow_fft; 1-D r2c 2.50x and c2r 2.75x vs upstream, 1.45x and 1.44x vs FFTW_ESTIMATE; 2-D c2c 6.43x vs FFTW_ESTIMATE. Slower than FFTW_MEASURE (0.71x for 1-D c2c) and KFR (0.49x). 2-D and 3-D versus upstream PocketFFT are about 1.0x.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the READMEs: benchmarks use CXX/CXXFLAGS from the Makefile environment; FFTW 3.3.10 built from the release tarball; KFR 7 built with clang++ C++20; SIMD and no-SIMD builds
tradeoffs: Header-only C++11 like PocketFFT; the tuning targets hot 1-D paths (large power-of-two c2c terminal stages, fused pass4x4, split8 buffering, measured dispatch for selected mixed radix). Keeps PocketFFT features (float/double/long double, multi-dimensional, DCT/DST, Bluestein).
caveats: First-party benchmark by the fork author. CPU model is not stated; the workstation was not quiet (ASLR on, load average often above idle) and the author calls the numbers a local snapshot. The fork loses to FFTW_MEASURE and KFR on most 1-D cases and to upstream on some 2-D/3-D cases. MKL is not in the harness. Fork changes performance-relevant code, so it is reported here, but the orchestrator may fold it under PocketFFT. Floating-point precision of the runs is not stated in the README.
found_via: GitHub: mcp github search_repositories query 'pocketfft' (sorted by stars) listed Dimandragon/pocketfft-tuned 'benchmark-driven optimized fork of pocketfft'

name: dft_simd (vertical-SIMD FFTW codelets for batched short DFTs)
baseline: FFTW3 plan/execute API (single DFT per execute, aligned; also 8 per execute and transposed variants)
workload: Transform 2^24 (16.8 million) short waveforms on one core: 60-sample real-to-complex (AVX2) and a 1024-point codelet (AVX2 and AVX512); FFTW API calls versus FFTW genfft-generated codelets recompiled to run on AVX vectors holding 8 (or 16) different waveforms.
claimed_speedup: 2025 update, AMD EPYC 9474F single core: 60-sample AVX2 codelet 149 ms (fixed-stride variant 79 ms) vs FFTW_Aligned_One 858 ms (README: 10.8x for the best variant); 1024-sample AVX2 codelet 9,124 ms (fixed stride 7,270 ms) vs 12,136 ms (README: about 1.6x); 1024-sample AVX512 codelet 12,628 ms (fixed stride 10,610 ms) vs 24,657 ms (README: 2.3x). 2018 Xeon E5-2650 v4: AVX codelet 220 ms vs FFTW3 2,194 ms for 1 waveform per call (about 10x, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: CMakeLists: -march=native -std=c++11 -O3 (the -O3 is added for Release builds); README names gcc 4.8.5 for the Xeon run and Apple LLVM 9.0.0 for the laptop run; compiler of the 2025 EPYC run not stated
hardware: AMD EPYC 9474F single core (2025 update); Intel Xeon E5-2650 v4; MacBook Pro Intel Core i5-5287U 2.9 GHz
tradeoffs: Only helps when many same-size small transforms are batched and the data can be laid out so each SIMD lane holds a different waveform (vertical layout). Codelets must be generated with FFTW's OCaml genfft and compiled in advance; code size grows as N log N; there is no planner for large sizes. GPL because it derives from FFTW genfft output.
caveats: The baseline is FFTW's general API on the same batch, not a hand-tuned FFTW batched SIMD path. FFTW version is not stated (MacPorts install on the laptop run). The original tests used only N=60; the author says conclusions depend on compiler and CPU. Build type must be Release for -O3 to apply. The 2025 table is the only one with the EPYC and has no compiler line.
found_via: GitHub: mcp github search_code query '"outperforms FFTW"' returned sfegan/dft_simd README.md

name: SFFT3 (3-D FFT built from FFTW 1-D transforms)
baseline: FFTW3 own 3-D routines (FFTW_PATIENT on the Ryzen table, FFTW_MEASURE on the i7 table)
workload: Average time of a forward plus reverse 3-D real FFT from 64^3 to 2100x2100x121 (and 2048x2048x1024), one OpenMP thread per physical core, padding and planning time excluded; SFFT3 uses FFTW's 1-D routines with cache-blocked transposes and a per-thread workspace.
claimed_speedup: 8-core Ryzen 3700X: 512^3 8.428e-2 s vs FFTW3-P 1.009e-1 s (1.20x, derived from page data); 1024^3 7.733e-1 s vs 1.011 s (1.31x, derived); 256^3 1.112e-2 vs 1.213e-2 s; slower at 64^3 (1.821e-4 vs 1.185e-4 s) and 128^3. 4-core i7-6700K vs FFTW_MEASURE: 512^3 0.182 vs 0.196 s (1.08x, derived), 1024^3 1.640 vs 1.705 s (1.04x, derived), slower at 128^3 and 2100x2100x121.
compiler_and_flags: gcc (version and optimization flags not stated in the README); i7 run built with CFLAGS=-DSFFT3_L2=256000
tradeoffs: Not an independent FFT: it calls FFTW3 for every 1-D transform (GPL). Uses a larger workspace than FFTW's 3-D plans (author says timings are not directly comparable). No explicit vectorization, no auto-tuning; L1/L2 sizes are compile-time constants.
caveats: Author calls it an untested proof-of-concept run on two similar machines and expects the results not to generalize; wins are 4-31% on large cubes and it loses at small sizes. Compiler version, flags and FFTW version are not stated.
found_via: GitHub: mcp github search_code query '"vs FFTW" filename:README.md' followed by a 'faster than FFTW' README search surfaced elgw/sfft3

name: MPSFT (Matrix Pencil Sparse Fourier Transform)
baseline: FFTW (built from source; FFTW_ESTIMATE and FFTW_MEASURE)
workload: Single-core transform of a length-N signal with S non-zero frequencies (sparse spectrum): N=2^22 with S from 64 to 4096, and S=50 with N from 8191 to 16,777,213.
claimed_speedup: README: for N=2^22 faster than FFTW when S is below around 1800. Numbers: MPSFT 19.4 ms at S=64, 75.8 ms at S=512, 140.8 ms at S=1024, 263.4 ms at S=2048; FFTW at N=4194304 225.3 ms in the first set (FFTW_ESTIMATE per README) and 102.3 ms in the second set (FFTW_MEASURE per README). Derived from page data: 5.3x faster than FFTW_MEASURE at S=64, break-even against FFTW_MEASURE between S=512 and S=1024.
compiler_and_flags: Bazel --config=opt from src/.bazelrc: g++ -std=c++11 -O3 -ffast-math -mavx2 -mtune=native -fopenmp-simd; CPU scaling disabled; FFTW built from source with --enable-shared --enable-threads --enable-openmp
tradeoffs: Approximate sparse Fourier transform: only valid when the spectrum is S-sparse (plus noise); probabilistic with tuned window and iteration parameters. Needs FFTW for small FFTs plus Eigen and Boost.SIMD; single-threaded. Not a general FFT replacement.
caveats: CPU model not stated. The wins hold only for sparse spectra and moderate S. The mapping of the two FFTW result blocks to ESTIMATE and MEASURE follows the README sentence order. A linked report (report/report.pdf) and an MIT thesis hold the accuracy results, not opened. GPL-2.0 text is in src/COPYING.txt; the README says GPL and plans to drop the FFTW dependency (KissFFT).
found_via: GitHub: mcp github search_code query '"faster than FFTW" filename:README.md' listed jiaweichiu/mpsft; earlier WebSearch 'github sparse FFT sFFT faster than FFTW sparse Fourier transform implementation code' also surfaced it

name: FINUFFT (Flatiron Institute nonuniform FFT, CPU and GPU)
baseline: NFFT3 (Chemnitz NFFT), CMCL NUFFT, MIRT, BART NUFFT (nonuniform FFT incumbents, not FFTW itself)
workload: Types 1, 2 and 3 nonuniform FFTs in 1-3 dimensions at requested tolerances, compared in the nufft-bench MATLAB harness and the 2019 SIAM J. Sci. Comput. paper (Barnett, Magland, af Klinteberg).
claimed_speedup: docs/related.rst: NFFT 'significantly slower and/or more memory-intensive than FINUFFT'; CMCL NUFFT 'much (up to 50x even for one thread) slower'; MIRT 'slower than FINUFFT for all tolerances smaller than 10^-1'; DUCC 'in some regimes is faster than ours'. Legacy cuFINUFFT README: up to 10x over CPU FINUFFT and up to 100x faster than other established GPU NUFFT codes.
compiler_and_flags: nufft-bench README: GCC 7.3.0 (NFFT built with GCC 6.4.0), CMCL rebuilt with -fPIC -Ofast -funroll-loops -march=native; FINUFFT flags not stated there
stars_or_usage: 445 stars; used through jax-finufft, python bindings and nifty-ls
tradeoffs: Solves a different problem from uniform FFT libraries: nonuniform points, a tolerance parameter, spreading kernel. Uses FFTW or DUCC for the inner uniform FFT, CUDA for the GPU path. C, Fortran, MATLAB, Python and Julia interfaces.
caveats: The tier B rests on the peer-reviewed 2019 paper cited in the README; the paper itself could not be opened here (arXiv and SFU hosts blocked), and the page cited gives only the quotes above. ahbarnett/nufft-bench (the benchmark harness) says MIRT's apply step beats all others in 1-D and 2-D, and MIRT precomputation is very expensive. Benchmarks date from 2018-2019. Baselines are not FFTW, MKL or KissFFT, and the category fit (NUFFT) is loose.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'FINUFFT github flatironinstitute benchmark faster than NFFT nonuniform FFT'; mcp github search_repositories 'nufft'; related.rst and nufft-bench README opened for the claims

name: FastAndFourier (FAF, JIT-compiled DSP/FFT library)
baseline: KissFFT (and FFTW3 FFTW_ESTIMATE/FFTW_MEASURE, which beat it); also NotoriousFFT
workload: Single-transform C2C latency in double precision at N=8 to 65536, first on macOS x86_64 (2026-02-22) and then Linux aarch64 interleaved FP64 (2026-09-03).
claimed_speedup: x86_64 macOS, 2.3 GHz AVX2: at N=65536 907 us vs KissFFT 3253 us (README: 3.2-3.6x faster; 3.6x derived from page data) but slower at N=64 (4.40 vs 1.11 us), 1024 (75.3 vs 27.1 us) and 16384 (1595 vs 634 us); FFTW3 measure is 3-10x faster than everything. Linux aarch64 6 x 1.73 GHz: 53.8 ns vs 95.3 ns at N=8, 0.778 vs 0.850 at N=64, 16.5 vs 21.7 at N=1024, 2238 vs 2735 at N=65536 (slightly slower at N=16: 0.161 vs 0.149).
compiler_and_flags: -O3 -march=native -ffast-math -funroll-loops for the x86 run (README); -O3 -march=native for the aarch64 run; compiler name not stated
hardware: x86_64 2.3 GHz with AVX2 under macOS Ventura and Linux aarch64 6 x 1.73 GHz; CPU models not named
tradeoffs: Runtime JIT: transforms are lowered to C and compiled by a system C compiler (falls back to a VM interpreter without one). Sizes up to 2^16, 5-smooth sizes plus codelets and Rader primes, optional Bluestein. Part of a larger DSP library with a scripting language, DWT and CWT.
caveats: The README itself says FFTW3 wins at nearly every size and that small N is not the library's race (about 1 us VM floor); the win over KissFFT on x86 only appears at N=65536 and on aarch64 at four of five sizes. The README flags the x86 table as the old VM-floor result. First-party numbers, CPU models not named. NotoriousFFT, by the same author, is faster than FAF on aarch64 by 1.2-2.15x. Possible duplicate decision with Notorious-FFT.
found_via: GitHub: mcp github search_code query '"faster than kissfft"' returned NotoriousLOB/FastAndFourier README.md

name: Notorious-FFT
baseline: minfft (aimukhin/minfft, small power-of-two FFT library; not one of the listed incumbents)
workload: Forward and inverse complex DFT, real DFT and DCT-2 in double precision at N=16 to 65536, built with the repo's bench target.
claimed_speedup: README: v1.0.0 beats minfft by 1.08-1.13x on complex forward DFT for N>=256 (N=1024 13.86 us vs 15.23 us; N=4096 68.95 us vs 77.59 us); inverse up to 1.18x at N=4096; real DFT 1.01-1.07x for N>=256; N=16 tied (0.97x); slightly slower at some small real sizes (0.83x at N=16).
tradeoffs: FFTW3-shaped planner API and FFTW compatibility header, split-radix DIF with mixed radix 3/5/7, Rader and Bluestein, DCT/DST types 2-4, NEON, AVX2 and AVX-512 paths selected at compile time.
caveats: Baseline minfft is a small niche library (53 stars), not FFTW, MKL or KissFFT; margins are 8-13%. Only an ARM machine is measured, the AVX2/AVX-512 paths have no published numbers. The README names a comprehensive benchmark against FFTW3, KissFFT, PocketFFT and muFFT but publishes no results. A Bluestein AVX inverse twiddle bug was fixed in Aug 2026.
found_via: GitHub: WebFetch of github.com/NotoriousLOB/Notorious-FFT after the WebSearch 'github header-only FFT AVX2 AVX-512 "faster than FFTW" benchmark KissFFT pocketfft' result list

name: OFFT
baseline: FFTW 3.3.5 (FFTW_ESTIMATE, with and without SIMD) and Intel oneMKL
workload: Complex FFT at powers of two (1024 to 2^24), powers of ten and 30 non-power-of-two lengths (1023 to 16777217); numbers are nanoseconds per n*ln(n), single table per size.
claimed_speedup: Author claim: for arbitrary sizes OFFT is often faster than FFTW, even the SIMD version. From the table, OFFT beats FFTW_ESTIMATE-with-SIMD at 10 of 30 non-power-of-two lengths (e.g. 1025: 6.7 vs 8.0; 4097: 6.0 vs 7.4; 262145: 9.0 vs 11.6; 16777217: 8.7 vs 12.3, i.e. 1.41x derived from page data) and is slower at powers of two (1024: 2.1 vs 0.5) and than MKL.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 12.2.0 (MSYS2) on Windows; optimization flags not stated
hardware: Intel i5-2450M 2.5 GHz laptop, SSE4 only, Windows 10
tradeoffs: C++11 header-style library for arbitrary-length transforms, no SIMD yet, code-generated kernels, keeps code size small.
caveats: Mixed result that the author's wording overstates: slower than FFTW_ESTIMATE at powers of two and at 19 of 30 non-power-of-two sizes (one tie), and slower than MKL; FFTW_MEASURE was deliberately not used. Old CPU, no SIMD in OFFT, optimization flags not stated, FFTW 3.3.5 Windows binaries. Author says numbers are noisy.
found_via: GitHub: mcp github search_repositories 'fft vectorized library C++' result list (christian-volmer/OFFT) then its doc/OfftSpeedComparison.md

name: SYLT-FFT (fixed-point FFT for Cortex-M4)
workload: 256-point inverse 32-bit fixed-point complex FFT on a Freescale Kinetis K20 (Cortex-M4).
claimed_speedup: +25.6% faster (Keil C 5.01 -O3) and +15.1% faster (GNU ARM 4.8.4 -O3) than arm_cfft_radix2_q31 for fft_inverse at N=256.
compiler_and_flags: Keil C Compiler 5.01 -O3; GNU Tools for ARM Embedded Processors 4.8.4 -O3
tradeoffs: 32-bit fixed-point radix-2 only, in place, no plan, tiny twiddle tables; DIT or DIF; optional rounding and saturation. Designed for speed, not accuracy; the caller must prevent overflow.
caveats: One data point (256-point inverse) against a 2014 CMSIS-DSP 1.4.2 library that predates later CMSIS FFT routines. License is the 'MHG' text: an Unlicense plus a non-binding moral-use condition, so non-standard. A forward-FFT DIT math error was fixed in Jan 2021. Benchmark code location is not given in the README.
found_via: GitHub: mcp github search_repositories query 'fft language:C' (sorted by stars), then the SYLT-FFT README

name: OTFFT (OK Ojisan's Template FFT)
workload: Stockham/mixed-radix complex FFT with AVX; project homepage compares against FFTW (and Ooura FFT) for lengths 2^1 to 2^24 (homepage not reachable from the research environment).
claimed_speedup: Project homepage title 'OTFFT -- FFT library using AVX that is faster than FFTW'; no numbers were available on any page opened here (the akinomyoga/OTFFT README only says the bundled fftbench programs need FFTW3 and Ooura's fftsg.c).
stars_or_usage: 29 stars (DEWETRON fork); akinomyoga/OTFFT OTFFT-6.5m fork 13 stars; included in kfrlib/fft-benchmark and used as the model for ZL-Audio/zldsp_fft
tradeoffs: C++ template metaprogramming makes builds slow; compile-time AVX selection; OpenMP six-step variant; DEWETRON fork adds CMake, multi-ISA builds (AVX2, AVX, SSE2) and unit tests; complex, real, DCT-II and Bluestein, sizes up to 2^24-2^25.
caveats: Tier D by necessity: the original homepage (wwwa.pikara.ne.jp) with the numbers was blocked, and neither fork's README has results, so the claim could not be checked. Please have the verifier open the homepage benchmark pages. The DEWETRON default branch last changed 2022-08-17 (repo metadata shows later activity); akinomyoga/OTFFT was updated 2025-09-03. Upstream homepage is not a GitHub repo, so the forks are the cited code.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'OTFFT github Okojisan FFT library AVX2 faster than FFTW' (result titles) and DEWETRON/otfft README via raw.githubusercontent.com
